source_testimonies.care:
Care-Ethics Reading of the Scene

1. Relational starting point  
   • All six people are strangers.  
   • No one has explicitly entrusted us with their care.  
   • The moment we notice the runaway trolley, attentiveness (Tronto, E1) triggers a situational responsibility: each person in danger now depends on whether we act or not.

2. Comparing the two possible actions through the same care dimensions  

              | Do nothing                    | Pull the lever
   ————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————
   Direct entrustment  | None                           | None
   Created vulnerability| We allow pre-existing danger   | We actively create a new fatal danger for one
   Ongoing dependency   | Five lives hinge on our inaction| One life hinges on our action; five hinge on our action to be spared
   Trust expectations  | All six can reasonably expect a passer-by to try to help | Same expectation
   Competent responsiveness| Fails to mitigate avoidable harm| Mitigates harm for five but inflicts fatal harm on one
   Responsiveness feedback| No chance for injured parties to respond| The one redirected victim has no say; the spared five cannot thank or object before the decision

3. Where the tension lies  
   • Do-nothing fails the phase of competence (E1): we stand by while five deaths could be prevented.  
   • Pulling the lever succeeds at competence toward five but simultaneously makes us the direct agent of the lone victim’s death, generating a new “agent-created vulnerability.”  

4. Weight of numerical magnitude  
   Designation: DECISIVE, because all other relational factors (strangers, equal dependency, no prior trust differential) are symmetrical. When relational stakes are otherwise tied, care ethics may let sheer numbers tip the scale—not as impersonal calculus, but because more people are counting on the carer’s responsiveness.

5. Provisional care-ethical judgment  
   • Attentiveness calls for a response.  
   • Responsibility and competence counsel acting to minimize the net abandonment of dependents.  
   • Responsiveness to the lone victim is tragically overridden, but not ignored: the choice still recognizes the harm and demands moral acknowledgment (grief, possible restitution to next of kin, self-reflection).

Care-Ethics Status: NORMATIVELY_CONTESTED, yet provisionally favoring pulling the lever.  
The relational claims are so closely matched that some care theorists might refuse to author a death they could not prevent otherwise. Still, given symmetrical relations, the greater number of dependents makes the lever pull the more responsive act of care.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.deontological:
Action: PULL_LEVER  
1. Maxim: “When I can save five strangers only by redirecting a threat so that it will kill one other stranger, I will do so.”  Universal test: If every rational agent willed this, each could be deliberately targeted whenever his death spares more; the very security of persons would be undermined. Not willable.  
2. Satisfies: rescue (save five). Violates: non-instrumentalization, autonomy, justice, truth (implicit claim the one may be used), impartiality (one singled out).  
3. Classification: PROHIBITED.  
4. Conflict: perfect duty not to intentionally kill vs imperfect duty to rescue. Priority rule: perfect duties override imperfect ones; coercive killing creates a stringent autonomy violation.  
5. Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY (shows size of rescue duty but cannot override a perfect right).  

Action: DO_NOT_PULL  
1. Maxim: “When an unavoidable threat will kill five strangers and intervention would require killing one, I refrain.” Universal test: All can rationally will this; no one is treated merely as a means. Willable.  
2. Satisfies: non-instrumentalization, autonomy, justice, truth, impartiality. Violates: rescue (fails to aid five).  
3. Classification: REQUIRED (imperfect rescue duty is outweighed by perfect duty not to kill).  
4. Duty conflict resolved as above: perfect > imperfect.  
5. Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY (illustrates gravity of omitted aid but does not override perfect duty).  

Deontological Status: DO_NOT_PULL REQUIRED; PULL_LEVER PROHIBITED.
source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Actions compared:  
A1 = “Pull the lever.”  
A2 = “Do not pull the lever.”

Least-advantaged group & basic liberty  
• A1: the single redirected victim is uniquely selected for death; she loses the basic liberty/right to life.  
• A2: the five already on the main track are those who die; they too lose the same basic liberty.

Liberty assessment  
Rawlsian CORE passage E2: “the loss of freedom for some is not made right by a greater good shared by others.”  Redirecting the trolley deliberately withdraws one person’s inviolability to benefit the rest.  A2 involves no comparable active infringement; the deaths are tragic but not produced by a new coercive choice that singles out a person.

Fair-equality-of-opportunity & difference principle  
Neither action distributes social advantages or opportunities; the primary issue is equal basic liberty (life).  Once a plan directly violates a person’s inviolability, the first principle blocks trade-offs, so second-principle reasoning never activates.

Numerical magnitude  
IRRELEVANT: head-count gains cannot override an individual’s inviolable basic liberty.

Rawlsian ranking  
Priority of equal basic liberty → A2 (“Do not pull the lever”) is ethically safer; A1 breaches the first principle.

Rawlsian Status: DETERMINATE – recommend A2.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Action-Consequence Table  

1. Pull lever (redirect to one)  
a. Person on side-track: death; probability 1; magnitude –100; permanent, irreversible; STATED  
b. Five on main track: spared; probability 1; magnitude +100 each; permanent; STATED  
c. Bystander (you): possible guilt/approval; probability HIGH; magnitude small (±5); lasting; INFERRED  
d. Public trust in intervention: minimal; UNKNOWN; magnitude small; reversible; UNKNOWN  

2. Do nothing  
a. Five on main track: death; probability 1; magnitude –100 each; permanent; STATED  
b. Person on side-track: unharmed; probability 1; magnitude 0; STATED  
c. Bystander (you): possible guilt/approval; probability HIGH; magnitude small (±5); INFERRED  

Impact ranking (probability × magnitude, absolute values):  
1) Lives of five (±500)  
2) Life of one (100)  
3) Bystander feelings (≈5)  
4) Societal trust (negligible, speculative)  

Comparison  
Pulling lever yields net +400 life-units (+500 saved –100 lost). Not pulling yields –500. Concrete, high-certainty effects on six people vastly outweigh all weaker, uncertain side-effects.  

Assumptions that could overturn result: if the lone person’s continued life would generate ≥4 times the aggregate welfare of the other five, or if saving the five imposes large hidden harms (e.g., riots), neither of which is stated. Probability of such reversal is UNKNOWN and unsupported.  

Utilitarian Principle (Edgeworth E1, Bentham E3): maximize total pleasure/avoid pain; justice (Mill E2) aligns because killing fewer minimizes overall suffering.  

Utilitarian Recommendation: Pull the lever. Utilitarian Status: DETERMINATE.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Action A: “Pull the lever”  
• Role: on-scene bystander suddenly entrusted with life-and-death power.  
• Virtues expressed: compassion for the five, resolute courage to act amid fear, responsibility for preventable harm.  
• Vices risked: hubris (playing fate’s judge), callousness toward the one, rashness if motives are merely numerical.  
• Circumstances noticed: instant timing, certainty of tracks, no other rescue, the one person’s innocence equal to the five’s.  
• Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—saving more lives counts, but only as one concern among just regard for each life.

Action B: “Do not pull the lever”  
• Role: same bystander, but choosing non-intervention.  
• Virtues expressed: humility before tragic limits, fidelity to the principle “do no direct harm,” steadiness against panic.  
• Vices risked: cowardly inaction, negligence toward avoidable deaths, moral evasiveness disguised as purity.  
• Circumstances noticed: identical facts; omission still foreseeably allows five deaths.  
• Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY for the same reason.

Central virtue conflict: compassion/beneficence toward many versus non-maleficence and respect for each individual life.

Practical-wisdom comparison rule: Prefer the option that best integrates compassion with responsibility while avoiding callousness or cowardice.

Provisional judgment: A practically wise, well-formed character would likely choose Action A, exercising courageous beneficence while sorrowfully acknowledging the tragic harm done to the one. Virtue-Ethics Status: NORMATIVELY_CONTESTED, yet Action A is the stronger candidate for human flourishing.
